Yet in recent years clinicians across the tropical world have become increasingly aware that the dengue virus can also attack the nervous system, producing encephalitis, spinal cord inflammation, and even paralysis in children. A team of radiologists at Aga Khan University Hospital in Karachi, Pakistan, has now compiled a systematic pictorial review of what pediatric dengue looks like on magnetic resonance imaging, organizing the findings by the underlying disease mechanisms that produce them. The review, published in Pediatric Radiology, is intended as a practical diagnostic atlas for physicians working in dengue-endemic regions, where recognizing these patterns quickly can change the course of a child’s illness. Pakistan has experienced repeated large dengue outbreaks, including a major epidemic in 2022 that prompted the World Health Organization to issue a formal disease outbreak notice. In such settings, children presenting with fever and new neurological symptoms pose a difficult diagnostic problem. The symptoms of dengue-related brain involvement, ranging from seizures and altered consciousness to weakness and confusion, overlap heavily with those of other viral encephalitides, autoimmune conditions, and metabolic derangements. Magnetic resonance imaging is often the decisive tool, but only if radiologists know which patterns to look for and how to distinguish them from close mimics. The Karachi group, led by Kumail Khandwala and Kiran Hilal, set out to fill that gap by illustrating the full spectrum of dengue-related neuroradiological findings in children and correlating each pattern with the published literature. The review’s central organizing principle is pathophysiology. Rather than listing findings haphazardly, the authors divide the imaging manifestations of pediatric dengue into three broad mechanistic categories: direct viral invasion of nervous tissue, immune-mediated injury, and reversible edema syndromes. This framework matters because the categories carry different prognoses and demand different clinical responses. Direct viral invasion tends to produce the most severe imaging abnormalities and the gravest illness, while the reversible edema patterns, as their name implies, often resolve completely with supportive care. Immune-mediated disease occupies an intermediate position, sometimes responding dramatically to immunomodulatory treatment. Understanding which category a given scan belongs to is therefore not an academic exercise but a practical step toward appropriate management. Within the direct-invasion category, the review describes meningoencephalitis, involvement of the deep gray matter nuclei, and rhombencephalitis, which is inflammation centered on the brainstem. The most striking and diagnostically valuable findings in this group are two named signs that have become associated with severe dengue encephalitis. The first is the so-called double doughnut sign, in which symmetric lesions in the thalami develop a central area of necrosis surrounded by a ring of edema, producing a pattern on axial images that resembles two doughnuts side by side. This appearance reflects acute necrotizing encephalopathy, a fulminant form of viral brain injury in which the damage is driven partly by a cytokine storm rather than by the virus alone. The review notes that dengue-associated acute necrotizing encephalopathy is now considered by many investigators to be a true variant of that syndrome rather than a mere mimic, a conclusion supported by a recent systematic review of published cases. The second named pattern is the Jack-o’-lantern sign, seen in dengue rhombencephalitis. On imaging, the brainstem shows scattered, patchy areas of abnormal signal within the pons that give the structure a carved, hollowed-out appearance reminiscent of a Halloween pumpkin. Brainstem involvement in dengue is uncommon but clinically dangerous, because the pons and medulla control breathing, heart rate, and other vital functions. The review highlights that this sign has been reported to be reversible in some patients who survive the acute illness, which underscores the importance of recognizing it early and providing aggressive supportive care rather than assuming a uniformly fatal course. Distinguishing dengue rhombencephalitis from other causes of brainstem inflammation, such as Listeria infection or other flaviviruses, relies on the clinical context, serological testing, and the specific distribution of lesions. The immune-mediated category encompasses two related but distinct white matter disorders. The first is acute leukoencephalopathy with restricted diffusion, a condition in which the brain’s white matter shows marked restriction of water molecule movement on diffusion-weighted imaging, indicating acute cytotoxic injury. The second is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a post-infectious autoimmune demyelinating syndrome in which the body’s immune response, triggered by the virus, mistakenly attacks the myelin sheaths of its own neurons. The review emphasizes that these two entities can be told apart by their diffusion characteristics and their timing relative to the infection. Acute leukoencephalopathy with restricted diffusion typically appears during the acute phase and shows true restricted diffusion, whereas acute disseminated encephalomyelitis tends to emerge days to weeks after the febrile illness and shows different diffusion behavior along with lesions that may enhance after contrast administration. This distinction has direct therapeutic consequences, because the autoimmune condition is the one that typically warrants corticosteroids or other immunotherapy. The third category, reversible edema syndromes, includes two entities with reassuring outcomes when properly identified. Reversible splenial lesion syndrome involves a characteristic lesion in the splenium, the posterior portion of the corpus callosum that connects the brain’s two hemispheres. On MRI the lesion appears as a small, round area of restricted diffusion, and, crucially, it typically disappears completely on follow-up imaging as the child recovers. Dengue has been reported as a cause of this syndrome in multiple case reports from Asia and elsewhere. The second, less commonly reported entity in the dengue context is posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, a condition in which the parietal and occipital regions of the brain develop vasogenic edema, often in association with severe hypertension, seizures, and visual disturbances. The Karachi group has previously studied pediatric posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in depth, examining how blood pressure relates to imaging severity and atypical MRI features, and that expertise informs the current review’s treatment of the dengue-associated form. Beyond the brain, the review extends its atlas to the spinal cord and peripheral nerves. Dengue-associated myelitis, inflammation of the spinal cord, can produce transverse myelitis with weakness and sensory loss below the affected level, and MRI plays a central role in defining the extent and character of the cord lesion. Guillain-Barré syndrome, the autoimmune peripheral neuropathy that causes ascending weakness and can progress to respiratory failure, has also been increasingly linked to dengue infection, with recent systematic reviews cataloging the clinical characteristics, outcomes, and predictors of severity in these patients. The review stresses that MRI is valuable in differentiating dengue-related myeloradiculopathies from other infectious and inflammatory causes, a distinction that determines whether antiviral, immunomodulatory, or purely supportive strategies are most appropriate. Perhaps the most practically useful single insight in the review concerns hemorrhage. The authors highlight that intralesional hemorrhagic changes, detected on susceptibility-weighted imaging or gradient recalled echo sequences, particularly within the deep gray nuclei and the brainstem, represent a valuable marker that favors dengue over several viral and inflammatory mimickers. Susceptibility-weighted sequences are exquisitely sensitive to blood breakdown products, and their ability to reveal microhemorrhages in characteristic locations gives radiologists an additional clue that can tip the diagnostic balance in dengue’s favor. In a region where Japanese encephalitis, tuberculosis, and other neurotropic infections circulate alongside dengue, such pattern-recognition tools can meaningfully shorten the path to the correct diagnosis. The broader significance of the Karachi review lies in its synthesis. By systematically illustrating the full range of pediatric dengue neuroradiology and anchoring each pattern in its pathophysiological mechanism, the authors aim to improve diagnostic confidence among radiologists and clinicians who may encounter only a handful of such cases in a career. As climate change expands the geographic range of the Aedes mosquito vectors and dengue incidence rises globally, the neurological complications of the virus will increasingly be seen outside traditional endemic zones, in emergency departments where familiarity with these imaging signatures is limited. A pattern-based approach, grounded in the double doughnut and Jack-o’-lantern signs, the diffusion characteristics that separate leukoencephalopathy from demyelination, and the hemorrhagic markers that distinguish dengue from its mimics, offers a practical framework for timely recognition and management of one of the more feared complications of a rapidly spreading tropical disease. Read Full Bio Ana Maria Soler, Joan Murray Joan Murray Joan Murray is an Emmy-winning journalist who has reported for CBS News Miami for over two decades. Read Full Bio Joan Murray Updated on: October 6, 2026 / 8:37 PM EDT / CBS Miami Add CBS News on Google Florida health officials have confirmed a human case of locally acquired dengue fever in Broward County, prompting a mosquito-borne illness advisory for the county amid rainy, humid conditions fueling a rise in mosquito populations. The Florida Department of Health in Broward County (DOH-Broward) and Broward County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance, prevention, and control efforts following the confirmed case. It is unknown what the age and gender are, the severity of the case, and where in Broward County the infected person lives. The case comes as Florida reported its largest dengue outbreak in several decades in the continental United States, with most of the cases coming from Hillsborough County, including the death of an elderly Tampa woman. Dengue fever is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito and is not contagious between people. Symptoms typically appear within 14 days of a bite and can present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches, joint pain, high fever, and occasionally a rash, though it generally does not cause respiratory symptoms. "Dengue is unique — not like other respiratory illnesses. Not a cough, but fever and abdominal [pain], in rare cases bleeding," said Broward Health ER physician Dr. Craig Harrison. Harrison noted that symptoms can take up to two weeks to appear, the virus is not contagious, and it is rarely life-threatening, though it can cause muscle and joint pain. Health officials advise residents to take basic precautions to avoid mosquito bites: Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants to cover exposed skin. Use Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellents on exposed skin and clothing. EPA-registered repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Remove standing water from buckets, garbage cans, pool covers, coolers, toys, flowerpots, or any containers where rainwater or sprinkler water collects. Repair any damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Statewide, the health department reports more than 250 locally acquired dengue cases, meaning individuals were bitten within Florida rather than while traveling. Bill Robles, owner of AAA Pest Control in Pompano Beach, emphasized that eliminating standing water is key during the rainy season. Many modern pesticides are non-toxic and formulated with plant oils such as lemongrass, cinnamon, and garlic. Technician M.J. sprays not only properties but also walks and fences. "When you spray the walls and fences, mosquitoes die and stay away," Robles said. Anyone experiencing symptoms is asked to contact DOH-Broward at 954-213-0710. The Associated Press contributed to this report. records.content_title: Da Nang sees surge in dengue cases as dangerous virus strain spreads
records.content: Thursday, October 8, 2026 Sign in Hello, Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Vietnam News Ho Chi Minh City Travel Economy Education Expat Life World Video Photo Vietnam News Sunday, October 4, 2026, 16:17 GMT+7 Da Nang sees surge in dengue cases as dangerous virus strain spreads 3:22 0.5x0.75x1.00x1.25x1.5x femalemale Da Nang City in central Vietnam had recorded more than 4,200 dengue fever cases as of October 1, up 2.4-fold year on year, with a large proportion of infections caused by a virus strain associated with a higher risk of severe disease. A dengue patient hospitalized in Da Nang City, central Vietnam. Photo: Truong Trung / Tuoi Tre The number of dengue outbreak clusters has risen sharply, reaching 283, marking a year-on-year increase of nearly fourfold, according to the Da Nang Center for Disease Control. The city has been reporting an average of about 350 dengue cases a week in recent weeks. Although the number of new cases declined slightly last week, it remained higher than both the five-year average and the level seen during the same period in 2025, said Dr. Nguyen Dai Vinh, director of the center. “The central region is entering the rainy season, so the outbreak could continue to intensify,” Vinh said. Inspection teams have been dispatched to areas where dengue case numbers are rising, he said. Laboratory testing has revealed a notable finding in this year’s outbreak: the predominance of the DENV-2 strain. Between January and September, 39 of 56 positive samples (70 percent) belonged to the DENV-2 serotype, according to the center. DENV-2 is considered a strain associated with a higher risk of severe dengue and potentially fatal complications. A health worker sprays disinfectant at a dengue cluster in Ngu Hanh Son Ward, Da Nang City, central Vietnam. Photo: Supplied Intensive campaign to eliminate mosquito breeding sites The center said one of its immediate priorities is to strengthen surveillance and promptly respond to individual cases and small outbreak clusters across the city. The onset of the rainy season creates favorable conditions for mosquitoes that transmit dengue to reproduce and spread. Without effective control of breeding sites, the risk of new outbreaks is expected to increase. Over the weekend, authorities in Ngu Hanh Son Ward mobilized residents to eliminate mosquito larvae and breeding sites. The ward also carried out a second round of disinfectant spraying in several areas where outbreaks had been detected. Local authorities said prevention efforts were not limited to spraying disinfectant after an outbreak emerged. RELATED NEWS Vietnam's Dak Lak records first dengue death of 2026 Vietnam warns of rising dengue cases as peak season begins Residents were also urged to turn over containers that could collect water and clear vegetation around their homes to prevent mosquitoes from breeding. The Da Nang Department of Health told Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper that it had established inspection teams to monitor infectious-disease prevention and control measures in eight communes and wards: Ngu Hanh Son, Son Tra, Hoa Khanh, An Khe, Kham Duc, Thanh My, Dai Loc, and Dien Ban Bac. The inspection campaign will continue through October 7. The center stressed that dengue prevention cannot rely solely on disinfectant spraying once an outbreak occurs. Eliminating mosquito breeding grounds, particularly water containers containing mosquito larvae, remains a key community-level prevention measure. records.content: Get the latest news from your city Download Thu, Oct 8, 2026Updated 05:39 AM IST Home Video Search Watch Top News Local National Cricket Business Originals International Tech & Science Entertainment Lifestyle Sports Utility Career Navaratri 2026 REELSNEW West Bengal Madhya Pradesh Uttar Pradesh Rajasthan Download App from Follow us on English News Local Gujarat Dengue Outbreak In Gandhinagar; CRPF Jawan Dies Amid Security Concern Dengue outbreak hits Ekta Parade personnel in Gandhinagar:Over 100 troops sick, suspected CRPF death raises security concerns Gandhinagar9 hours ago Copy link The dengue outbreak has become serious among paramilitary personnel who have arrived in Gandhinagar for the upcoming National Unity Day parade, with more than 100 personnel from the BSF, CRPF and ITBP contracting the vector-borne disease after being accommodated in new government housing complexes in Sectors 28 and 29. The situation is so severe that more than 55 sick personnel have been admitted to Gandhinagar Civil Hospital for treatment. CRPF jawan Amal Barman dies tragically during treatment The sudden death of 29-year-old CRPF jawan Amal Barman, who was undergoing treatment for dengue at the civil hospital, in suspicious circumstances has caused major concern among the security forces and local administration. According to details received, jawan Amal Barman's condition suddenly deteriorated last night during treatment. Arrangements were being made to shift him from the general ward to the emergency department immediately, but he died tragically before that could happen. The body was subjected to a post-mortem in the morning, and viscera samples have been sent for testing to determine the exact cause of death. Prima facie, the death is suspected to have been caused by severe dengue or cardiac arrest, although the actual cause will become clear only after the forensic report is received. Health Minister Holds High-Level Meeting and Orders Immediate Measures In view of the serious situation caused by the outbreak among the personnel, Health Minister Praful Pansheriya held an immediate high-level review meeting. The minister claimed that orders had been issued to carry out fogging, spray medicines and conduct intensive surveillance in the affected areas on a war footing. As a precautionary measure, four health workers have been specially assigned to each block of the personnel's residential area. In addition, strict instructions have been issued to ensure that water does not accumulate anywhere in the housing complex. The administration's shortcomings exposed amid government claims While the outbreak is spreading, the state Health Department has claimed that malaria and dengue cases have declined this year compared with last year and that more than 1.39 crore blood samples have also been tested. However, the alarming dengue situation among personnel deployed for national security in the heart of the capital, Gandhinagar, has exposed the administration's lack of preparedness. The incident has raised serious questions about the functioning and claims of the local administration. . records.content_title: Florida dengue cases hit record 252 as outbreak accelerates
records.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue cases hit record 252 as outbreak accelerates Florida reports 62 new locally-acquired dengue cases in one week Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 2, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET Florida reported 62 new locally acquired cases of dengue fever — sometimes called breakbone fever — in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. That brings the statewide total to 252 for the year as of Sept. 26, surpassing the previous highest number of cases in recent memory, which was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County. The Tampa Bay Times identified the victim as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection Hillsborough County continues to lead the state with 223 confirmed cases, while other locally acquired cases have been reported in six other counties. Three counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. Currently, 12 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. West Nile virus and chikungunya — which are also transmitted by mosquitoes — have also been reported in Florida this year, but in far fewer numbers than dengue. One human case of West Nile was reported in Alachua County in the period of Sept. 20-26, bringing the state total to six for the year. No new chikungunya cases were reported. ➤ Dengue cases keep climbing in Florida. This is how to protect yourself There have also been 245 dengue cases associated with international travel reported in Florida this year, 201 of which were from travel from Cuba, according to the FDOH. Most of the cases were reported in Miami-Dade County. Although these cases were not locally acquired, mosquitoes that bite infected people in the state can transmit the disease to others. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. Dengue continues to surge in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 26, there have been 252 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 190 reported Sept. 19. There have also been six positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 252 cases 223 in Hillsborough County 13 in Pinellas County 8 in Miami-Dade County 3 in Orange County 3 in Pasco County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 6 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. The factors that create ideal conditions for the mosquitoes responsible for transmitting the viruses include: Warmer temperatures: Summer high temperatures speed up mosquito life cycles and virus replication, allowing more mosquito generations in a single season and able to transmit viruses faster. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. "While dengue and chikungunya are not endemic in Florida, Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that transmits these viruses, is distributed primarily throughout south and central Florida. Tourists and travelers get infected with dengue or chikungunya outside of Florida then come to or return to Florida and get bit by the Aedes aegypti here, leading to infected mosquitoes present in Florida that can then potentially cause localized outbreaks of these viruses, like the dengue outbreak we are currently seeing in Tampa Bay." 12 Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Brevard Leon Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." All Florida residents could take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. These under-$25 October Prime Day deals end soon Woman Says Dengue ‘Felt like My Bones Were Breaking’ amid Deadly Outbreak in Florida Requinn Nicolette was hospitalized and sickened for four months after contracting the painful disease from a mosquito that bit her in her Lakeland, Fla., backyard By Cara Lynn Shultz Cara Lynn Shultz Cara Lynn Shultz is a writer-reporter at PEOPLE. Her work has previously appeared in Billboard and Reader's Digest. People Editorial Guidelines Published on October 5, 2026 11:32AM EDT Leave a Comment Add Us On Requinn Nicollette is sharing her experience with dengue as a warning. Credit : FOX 13 News/Youtube NEED TO KNOW Requinn Nicolette says a mosquito bite in her Lakeland backyard led to a four-month illness and hospitalization from dengue Florida has reported 252 locally acquired dengue cases this year, marking local spread for the first time in 15 years CDC advises residents in at-risk areas to use repellent and wear long sleeves and pants A Florida woman is sharing her experience with the brutal disease dengue fever amid a fatal surge of cases in the state. “It truly felt like my bones were breaking,” Requinn Nicolette told Fox 13 about her months-long struggle with dengue fever, which she says she contracted when a mosquito bit her in her Lakeland backyard two years ago. Dengue has earned the nickname “breakbone fever” due to the unbearable bone and muscle pain caused by the virus. The pain was “probably the worst symptom for me,” she said. The aspiring country singer said she’s sharing her story as a warning to be vigilant about preventing mosquito bites, as “I’m a grown adult and I can’t imagine a child experiencing what I experienced.” She endured a month of vomiting, a rash, and headaches. Her veins and blood vessels leaked internally, causing severe bruising. She was hospitalized for four days amid the four-month ordeal. “The bone pain and the muscle pain, it wouldn’t go away,” she told the outlet. Florida is dealing with an outbreak of the virus, which killed a Tampa woman, Gay Small, 80, in September. According to the most recent data from Florida Health, there have been a total of 252 locally acquired cases of dengue this year, with 62 cases reported in the week ending September 26. Related Stories Researchers Discover New Virus After Inventing a ‘Mosquito Toilet’ Officials Confirm Painful Mosquito-Borne Virus Back in U.S. After 6 Years Our new app is here! Free, fun and full of exclusives. Scan to download now! Most cases of dengue in the U.S. occur in people who contracted the disease — which is caused by a virus spread by the bite of the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquito — elsewhere, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control (CDC) says. However, the disease is spreading locally in Florida for the first time in 15 years, meaning that people are being infected by mosquito bites in the state. Stock image of someone spraying themselves with mosquito repellant. Getty Take PEOPLE with you! Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the latest details on celebrity news, exclusive royal updates, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox. About 25% of those who are bitten by an infected mosquito will get sick, and cases can range from mild to severe. Per the CDC, symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body pains in the muscles and joints. Treatment includes acetaminophen, rest and fluids. The best way to treat dengue is to avoid dengue, the CDC says, advising those in at-risk areas to wear long sleeves and pants, and to use an insect repellent with DEET, Picaridin oil, lemon eucalyptus or para-menthane-diol. The latter two ingredients are not recommended for children under 3 years of age. Start your Independent Membership today. Join today Already a member? Log in Florida is experiencing its largest dengue outbreak in decades, with 252 locally acquired cases reported as of late September, among the highest totals seen in the continental U.S. in several decades. The vast majority of cases have been reported in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, where officials are ramping up mosquito-control efforts, according to the latest numbers released by state health officials. Florida has also recorded 245 travel-associated cases this year, while at least 13 Hillsborough County cases involved people who had recently traveled. The surge has prompted Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties to declare local states of emergency and step up efforts to kill mosquitoes and eliminate standing water where they breed. Florida's locally acquired case total has already surpassed the state's previous annual high of just under 200 cases, reported in 2023. The current outbreak also appears to be the largest reported by a state in the continental U.S. in a single year since at least the 1940s, based on available state health department data. The total is nearing the 264 locally acquired cases reported in Hawaii over six months in 2015 and 2016, the largest outbreak reported by a U.S. state in decades. Federal health officials have cautioned that national dengue surveillance data is limited. open image in gallery Florida has reported more than 250 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, which is spread primarily by infected mosquitoes, becoming the U.S. continental state with the most reports in decades Dengue is a viral infection spread primarily through bites from infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, both of which are found in Florida. Some people have no symptoms, while others can develop a sudden fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea or vomiting. Most people recover, but dengue can sometimes become severe, causing bleeding, shock and death. Florida has reported one dengue-related death this year, involving an elderly Tampa woman who died on September 4. Most dengue cases reported in the continental U.S. are linked to international travel. Local transmission has occurred in several states, including Florida, Texas, Hawaii, Arizona and California, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Florida regularly sees travel-associated dengue because of its large number of international travelers. Public health experts say it remains unclear why the record dengue outbreak has been concentrated around Tampa rather than its historical epicenter in South Florida, NBC Miami reports. Travel patterns could play a role, while warmer temperatures and other climate conditions can create more favorable environments for mosquitoes. The CDC has provided Florida with $800,000 in emergency funding and is monitoring the outbreak. The agency has not sent disease investigators because state officials have not requested them. People in areas experiencing local transmission should use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear loose-fitting clothing that covers their arms and legs, and remove standing water around their homes, according to the CDC. The Florida outbreak comes as dengue continues to circulate at high levels globally. More than 2.2 million infections and nearly 1,200 deaths have been reported worldwide this year, according to the World Health Organization. The true number of infections may be higher because dengue can cause mild or no symptoms, meaning some people may never seek medical care or get tested. records.content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Entertainment Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Engine Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Florida is experiencing the largest dengue outbreak in decades in continental USA: over 250 local infections Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Saturday, October 3, 2026 - 1:08 PM Florida Beach (Reference image)Photo © CiberCuba The dengue outbreak affecting Florida in 2026 has become the largest recorded in the continental United States in at least eight decades, with over 250 confirmed cases of local transmission reported by week 38 of the year, according to the arboviral report from the Florida Department of Health. The figure surpasses the previous record set by the state itself, which dated back to 2023 with fewer than 200 local infections, and places Florida in an unprecedented scenario since the 1940s for any state in the continental territory. The most striking aspect of the outbreak is its geography: the epicenter is not in South Florida, where cases have historically been concentrated, but in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, which accounts for 223 of the more than 250 local infections reported throughout the state. For the first time this year, local transmission cases (252) have surpassed imported cases (245), indicating that the virus is circulating steadily among the local population and is not solely dependent on travelers returning from endemic areas. The authorities of Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas declared local states of emergency at the end of September, and Hillsborough County extended its declaration until October 8. Fogging crews are working day and night in neighborhoods such as South Tampa, Davis Islands, and Harbor Island to reduce the population of transmitting mosquitoes. The outbreak has already claimed a victim: an 80-year-old woman died in Tampa on September 4, marking the first dengue-related death in Florida in 2026. The focus of the outbreak began to emerge in July and has continued to grow since then. Dawn Wesson, an expert on dengue from Tulane University, warned that most residents in the Tampa area lack prior immunity to any form of the virus, making them especially vulnerable. She also noted that the shift of the outbreak towards Tampa may be related, at least in part, to the travel patterns in the area. Wesson also highlighted the absence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in the response to the outbreak: Florida has not requested the intervention of the federal agency's researchers, although the CDC provided $800,000 in assistance to the state health department. The regional context worsens the situation for Cubans in South Florida who frequently travel to the island. Cuba is expected to have around 7,133 estimated cases of dengue in 2026, a figure 7.4 times higher than the expected level for this time of year, according to the Global Dengue Observatory. The Cuban regime is also facing the simultaneous circulation of all four serotypes of the virus (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4), a combination that increases the risk of hemorrhagic forms, amid a healthcare collapse characterized by a shortage of fumigants, garbage accumulation, and a lack of drinking water. Chikungunya, reactivated on the island since July 2025, continues to circulate in 2026 according to alerts from the Ministry of Public Health itself. Those returning from Cuba or other Caribbean areas should exercise caution: use repellents registered by the Environmental Protection Agency containing ingredients like DEET, wear long-sleeved clothing, stay in air-conditioned spaces or areas with mosquito nets, and eliminate any accumulation of standing water at home, including in bottle caps or tires. The Aedes aegypti mosquito can bite at any time of day, although it is most active at dawn and dusk. Florida is also considering allowing pharmacists to administer the vaccine against chikungunya (VIMKUNYA, approved for those over 12 years old), although the measure has not yet been fully implemented. There is no dengue vaccine recommended for the general public in the continental U.S. Wesson bluntly summarized the looming horizon: "There is a good chance that this is the new normal." records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, October 4, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Hospitalisations Have Doubled in a Decade, Global Meta-Analysis Finds by Bioengineer October 2, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Dengue is quietly becoming one of the heaviest seasonal burdens on hospitals worldwide, and the most comprehensive assessment of its healthcare footprint in a decade suggests the strain is far greater than previously recognised. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in eClinicalMedicine has pooled real-world data from studies conducted between 2013 and 2026 and concluded that, globally, more than one in three patients with dengue is hospitalised, with the average admitted patient spending nearly five days in a hospital bed. The finding represents a striking increase over the last global estimate, published in 2016, which put the worldwide hospitalisation rate at just 18 percent. The research team, led by Namita Kaushik and Andreas Tietz, screened 6,983 records and identified 341 studies reporting healthcare resource utilisation or economic outcomes in dengue. Of these, 44 studies reporting hospitalisation rates and 121 studies reporting length of stay met the rigorous feasibility criteria for quantitative synthesis. The work followed PRISMA guidelines, was registered prospectively in the PROSPERO database, and applied the Downs and Black checklist to appraise study quality. Data were drawn from five biomedical databases searched via the Ovid platform, supplemented by citation searches and conference abstracts, with no restriction on country of origin. The headline result is a pooled global hospitalisation rate of 36.7 percent (95 percent confidence interval 29.0 to 44.4) among patients with dengue irrespective of severity, derived under a random-effects model. The mean length of stay across hospitalised patients was 4.9 days (95 percent CI 4.6 to 5.2). Both outcomes showed very high statistical heterogeneity, with I-squared values approaching 100 percent, reflecting the enormous diversity of settings, designs, and populations represented in the underlying literature. To understand that variation, the authors performed meta-regression across a range of study-level covariates, including geography, outbreak status, data source, and study design. Discover more Find Treatments Hospitalisations hospitalisation hospitalisations Hospitalisation One variable dominated all others: disease severity. Severity was significantly associated with both higher hospitalisation rates and longer stays, explaining 31.4 percent of between-study variance in hospitalisation and 11.4 percent of the variance in length of stay, with p-values below 0.0001 in both models. Subgroup analyses quantified the gradient precisely. Patients with non-severe dengue without warning signs were hospitalised at a pooled rate of 17.7 percent, rising to 36.9 percent once WHO warning signs such as persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, raised haematocrit, or thrombocytopaenia appeared. Among patients classified as having severe dengue, the pooled hospitalisation rate reached 79.4 percent. Length of stay followed the same severity gradient. Patients with non-severe disease averaged 4.6 days in hospital, compared with 6.5 days for severe dengue. The most dramatic figures emerged when complications were considered: patients with severe dengue or dengue haemorrhagic fever who developed complications such as shock, renal impairment, platelet-transfusion-requiring thrombocytopaenia, or sepsis stayed a mean of 15.5 days, roughly double the 7.5 days observed in severe cases without complications. Co-infections with pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2 or chikungunya virus, and comorbidities including haematologic malignancies, autoimmune disease, and obesity, each added roughly a day or more to the average stay. Regional patterns add a further layer of complexity. Hospitalisation rates were numerically higher in Asia, at 35.1 percent, than in Latin America, at 29.3 percent, and length of stay was correspondingly longer in Asian settings, at 5.1 days versus 4.1 days in Latin America. The authors note that this Asian excess echoes the 2016 analysis by Shepard and colleagues, which reported rates of 19.3 to 24.8 percent in Asian subregions against just 3.8 percent in Latin America and the Caribbean. Possible explanations include differing admission thresholds, a higher force of infection, multiple co-circulating serotypes, and demographic differences, but the authors emphasise that the drivers remain unclear and warrant targeted investigation. The timing of the analysis is significant. Since the last global estimates were published, the world has witnessed record-breaking dengue waves, shifts in circulating serotypes, changing patient demographics, the disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic, and improvements in surveillance and clinical preparedness. The World Health Organization reported a doubling of reported cases from around 7 million in 2023 to approximately 14 million in 2024, while modelling work published in 2025 estimated that annual apparent cases rose from 26.45 million in 1990 to 58.96 million in 2021. Against that epidemiological backdrop, a hospitalisation rate approaching 37 percent implies a demand for inpatient beds, nursing capacity, and supportive care that many endemic health systems are ill-equipped to absorb during peak transmission seasons. Discover more Check Symptoms Explore Data hospitals hospital Find Hospitals Methodological sensitivity analyses strengthen the central conclusions while exposing their limits. Excluding studies with fewer than 100 participants and those with more than 50,000 yielded a pooled hospitalisation rate of 29.4 percent with narrower confidence intervals, and excluding studies whose data were collected during the pandemic produced an estimate of 25.3 percent, hinting that overwhelmed COVID-era hospitals may have temporarily suppressed dengue admissions. A single exceptionally large nationwide Brazilian cohort dominated the fixed-effects estimate, but random-effects modelling, which the authors favoured given the heterogeneity, attenuated its influence. For length of stay, no evidence of publication bias was detected by Egger’s regression, and the GRADE certainty of evidence was rated low, primarily because of the observational design of the included studies rather than inconsistency or imprecision. The findings carry immediate practical implications. Hospitalisation is recognised as a key outcome in dengue research: an international Delphi consensus involving experts from more than 30 countries identified the need for hospitalisation as a core endpoint for patients and clinicians. The new benchmarks should therefore help clinical trialists select endpoints and calculate sample sizes, and they align with recently published WHO target product profiles that recommend dengue-related hospitalisation as a secondary efficacy outcome in non-severe disease. For policymakers, the estimates provide a foundation for cost-effectiveness analyses of vaccines, antivirals, and vector-control strategies, and for identifying the regions where preventive investment would relieve the greatest pressure on hospitals. The authors are careful to frame the pooled figures as average trends across highly diverse settings rather than universal constants. Admission thresholds, clinical practice, healthcare-seeking behaviour, and reporting conventions differ substantially between countries, and the denominator in most studies was skewed towards patients already seeking care, which may inflate the apparent hospitalisation rate relative to all symptomatic infections. The observation that some patients with warning signs or severe disease were nonetheless not hospitalised may reflect symptom misclassification, resource constraints, or emergency department stays that were never recorded as admissions. Even so, the overall message is difficult to escape: dengue’s demand on hospital infrastructure has likely risen considerably over the past decade, and quantifying the associated direct and indirect costs, productivity losses, and caregiver burden is now an urgent priority for global health planning. Redacción Clarín Share Follow Us 0 Comentar 05/10/2026 19:43 Florida is experiencing the largest statewide dengue outbreak in the United States in more than a decade, with more than 250 locally acquired cases and one death so far this year, according to Florida Department of Health data available Monday. The southern state recorded 252 local infections of the mosquito-borne virus through the 38th week of the year, which ended Sept. 26. Another 245 cases were imported, meaning they involved travelers who contracted the disease elsewhere, according to a Department of Health report. The outbreak is close to surpassing the 264 local cases Hawaii recorded over six months in 2015 and 2016. It could also break the record for the most infections of the virus in the continental United States since the 1940s, the local NPR affiliate reported. Pinellas, Pasco and Hillsborough counties declared emergency declarations The disease has prompted emergency declarations in three Florida counties: Pinellas, Pasco and Hillsborough. Hillsborough has become the epicenter of the outbreak, with 223 of the local cases. An Aedes aegypti mosquito with the dengue-blocking Wolbachia bacteria is seen at a laboratory in the Wolbito do Brasil plant in Curitiba, Parana state, Brazil September 1, 2025. REUTERS/Rodolfo Buhrer A month ago, Tampa, in Hillsborough County, reported the state's first dengue death of the year: an 80-year-old woman who had been bitten by a mosquito. The outbreak has drawn national attention. Although dengue is common in US territories such as Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands, infections are "limited" in continental states such as Florida, Texas, Arizona and California, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As of Monday, the CDC noted 485 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data. The World Health Organization (WHO) headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. REUTERS/Denis Balibouse/File Photo Global cases rose to 14.6 million in 2024, up from 505,430 in 2000, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), which warns that about half of the world's population is now at risk of contracting the virus. Last month, the WHO also urged countries affected by El Niño, a phenomenon marked by warmer-than-usual waters in the Pacific, to strengthen disease surveillance. El Niño could encourage the spread of mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue, malaria and Zika, even in previously unaffected areas. Dengue is transmitted through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito and does not spread from person to person. It causes fever and intense muscle and joint pain, and symptoms can appear up to 14 days after the bite. The data shows that the number of reported cases has risen in at least 15 states, with Florida accounting for the largest share of the increase. Florida Outbreak Continues to Grow The rise in national case numbers comes as Florida deals with an ongoing dengue outbreak that has drawn attention from public health officials. Florida has recorded hundreds of dengue infections this year, including a significant number of locally acquired cases, meaning people were infected within the state rather than while traveling abroad. The outbreak has been concentrated in the Tampa Bay region and has resulted in emergency declarations in several counties. What Is Dengue Fever? Dengue is a viral disease transmitted by infected mosquitoes. According to the CDC, symptoms can include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, rash, muscle pain, and joint pain. Most infections are mild, and many people develop no symptoms at all. However, some patients can develop severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition that can cause shock, severe bleeding, and organ failure. Why Are Cases Increasing? Public health experts have linked rising dengue activity in the United States to several factors, including international travel and the presence of Aedes mosquitoes, which are capable of transmitting the virus. Dengue is common in many tropical and subtropical regions. When travelers return to the United States while infected, local mosquito populations can sometimes spread the virus to other people. CDC Data Show Increases Across Multiple States The latest CDC data show reported case counts have risen since the agency's previous update. Florida posted by far the largest increase, with cases rising from 392 to 485, an increase of 93 cases. California recorded the second-largest increase, rising from 31 to 45 cases, an increase of 14. Other states showing increases were: Overall, the states listed in the CDC updates recorded a rise of 130 cases between the reporting periods. What Happens Next? Health officials continue to urge residents to reduce mosquito exposure by using EPA-registered insect repellents, wearing long sleeves, and eliminating standing water around homes where mosquitoes can breed. The latest CDC data suggest dengue activity remains elevated in Florida and is continuing to increase in a number of other states. While most U.S. cases are associated with travel, the Florida outbreak has demonstrated how quickly local transmission can develop when the virus is introduced into areas where dengue-carrying mosquitoes are present. Dengue is a viral disease transmitted by infected mosquitoes. According to the CDC, symptoms can include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, rash, muscle pain, and joint pain. Most infections are mild, and many people develop no symptoms at all. ... However, some patients can develop severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition that can cause shock, severe bleeding, and organ failure. Why Are Cases Increasing? Public health experts have linked rising dengue activity in the United States to several factors, including international travel and the presence of Aedes mosquitoes, which are capable of transmitting the virus. Dengue is common in many tropical and subtropical regions. When travelers return to the United States while infected, local mosquito populations can sometimes spread the virus to other people. CDC Data Show Increases Across Multiple States The latest CDC data show reported case counts have risen since the agency's previous update. View content https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30448290/ Florida posted by far the largest increase, with cases rising from 392 to 485, an increase of 93 cases. California recorded the second-largest increase, rising from 31 to 45 cases, an increase of 14. Other states showing increases were: New York: 27 to 31 (+4) Texas: 14 to 17 (+3) New Jersey: 16 to 19 (+3) Illinois: 10 to 13 (+3) Washington: 16 to 18 (+2) Maryland: 11 to 12 (+1) Connecticut: 6 to 7 (+1) Massachusetts: 10 to 11 (+1) Kentucky: 4 to 5 (+1) Indiana: 2 to 3 (+1) Nebraska: 2 to 3 (+1) Colorado: 10 to 11 (+1) West Virginia: 0 to 1 (+1) Overall, the states listed in the CDC updates recorded a rise of 130 cases between the reporting periods. What Happens Next? Health officials continue to urge residents to reduce mosquito exposure by using EPA-registered insect repellents, wearing long sleeves, and eliminating standing water around homes where mosquitoes can breed. The latest CDC data suggest dengue activity remains elevated in Florida and is continuing to increase in a number of other states. While most U.S. cases are associated with travel, the Florida outbreak has demonstrated how quickly local transmission can develop when the virus is introduced into areas where dengue-carrying mosquitoes are present. records.content: Quảng cáo của DTads Thursday, 08 October 2026 Tiếng Việt RSS VIETNAM TODAY Business Society Education Environment LIFESTYLE Travel Entertainment Food & Drink CULTURE AND SPORT Culture Sport COMMUNITY MULTI MEDIA Copied VIETNAM TODAY HCM City dengue cases top 35,700, high-risk groups warned October 03, 2026 - 07:19 PM HCM City has recorded more than 35,700 dengue cases so far this year, with health experts warning that infants, the elderly and pregnant women face higher risks of severe illness. The HCM City Centre for Disease Control (HCDC) said on October 3 that the city recorded 1,491 dengue cases in week 39, from September 21-27, broadly unchanged from the average of the previous four weeks. Cumulative cases since the beginning of 2026 have exceeded 35,700. Con Dao Special Zone and Chanh Phu Hoa and Minh Thanh wards recorded among the highest infection rates per 100,000 people. A child with severe dengue complications in HCM City (Photo: Hai An) At a recent HCDC seminar, experts highlighted three groups particularly vulnerable to severe dengue: older people, children, especially infants and those who are overweight, obese or have underlying conditions, and pregnant women. Dr Than Ha Ngoc The, vice chairman of the HCM City Geriatrics Association, said ageing weakens immune function and physiological reserves, while conditions such as hypertension and cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease can complicate treatment. Symptoms in older patients can also be atypical. Instead of high fever or pronounced aches, they may experience restlessness, drowsiness or confusion, making the disease harder to recognise. Dr Truong Huu Khanh, former head of the Infection-Neurology Department at Children's Hospital 1, said infants under one year old and children who are overweight, obese or have underlying conditions also face increased risks. Symptoms in infants can be difficult to detect before their condition suddenly deteriorates. Pregnant women require close monitoring because dengue can lead to complications including postpartum bleeding, premature birth and low birth weight. Experts warned that severe dengue can also affect young, healthy people. HCM City Hospital for Tropical Diseases recently treated critically ill patients aged 16 and 21, while a 20-year-old dengue patient died in September. The most dangerous phase of dengue typically occurs between the third and seventh days of illness, when fever may already have subsided. Without timely treatment, patients can develop shock or severe organ damage. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness, reduced urination and cold extremities. Older patients may also experience confusion or breathing difficulties. Health experts urged residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, prevent mosquito bites and seek medical attention promptly if symptoms develop. records.content: Florida case of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Broward County The Florida Department of Health in Broward County confirmed a human case of locally acquired dengue fever. The DOH-Broward also issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory, according to an Oct. 5 release, and said it is "coordinating surveillance, prevention, and control efforts" with Broward County Mosquito Control. According to the FDOH's Arbovirus Surveillance Report, "252 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from seven counties" as of Sept. 29, but none had previously been reported in Broward. Dengue, also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever for the pain it can cause, may present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the DOH-Broward. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses The DOH-Broward suggests area residents take the following steps to prevent being bitten: - "Wear protective clothing to prevent mosquito bites. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. - Apply insect repellents that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to exposed skin and clothing. When used as directed, EPA-registered insect repellents are proven safe and effective, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. - Control mosquitoes inside and outside. Repair damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Drain water from garbage cans, buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys, flowerpots, or any other containers where sprinkler or rainwater has collected." "Proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses include "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water," according to a June release by Miami-Dade County. It's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," the release read, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly spread by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: - Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. - Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." - Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. - Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. - Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. - Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county's online portal. Over 250 cases of locally acquired dengue in Florida this year More than 250 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report, with some in South Florida counties. The report for the period from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 says that "252 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from seven counties" in 2026. From Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 alone, 62 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, saw 223 of the 252 reported dengue cases this year. Miami-Dade County saw eight, Orange County saw three, Palm Beach County saw one, Pasco County saw three, Pinellas County saw 13 and Polk County saw one dengue case. Dengue continues to surge in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 26, there were been 252 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, up from the 190 reported Sept. 19. There have also been six positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. - Dengue: 252 cases - 223 in Hillsborough County - 13 in Pinellas County - 8 in Miami-Dade County - 3 in Orange County - 3 in Pasco County - 1 in Palm Beach County - 1 in Polk County - West Nile Virus: 6 cases - 2 in Alachua County - 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) - 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) - 1 in Walton County - Chikungunya: 1 case - 1 in Miami-Dade County Sarah Perkel is a South Florida Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network's Florida Connect team. records.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Tropical Storm Isaias World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Miami | News Weather Sports Videos Your Reporters 80° Local News Politics Consumer Health Entertainment Tech Lottery News Neighbors 4 Neighbors U.S. World NEXT Weather Tracking The Tropics Hurricane Preps All Sports CBS Sports HQ Dolphins Heat Panthers Marlins Miami FC Inter Miami FC Canes High School Sports Odds Meet Your Reporters Miami-Dade County News Broward County News Monroe County News Meet The Team Contact Us Station Info News Tips CBS Miami Shows Jim Berry's Absolutely Not Living With Parkinson's Miami Proud Making Ends Meet Contests & Promotions Galleries Advertise Download the App Jobs TV Schedule Watch CBS News U.S. Florida's dengue outbreak is now the largest in the continental US in decades, with over 250 reported cases Updated on: October 2, 2026 / 4:24 PM EDT / AP Add CBS News on Google Florida's current dengue outbreak appears to be the largest in several decades in the continental United States. State health officials reported this week that more than 250 locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne disease have been tallied so far this year. The vast majority of them were in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Federal health officials say their data on dengue outbreaks is limited. But available information from state health departments and medical journals suggests the Florida outbreak marks the most cases in a calendar year for any state since at least the 1940s. Puerto Rico is consistently hit hard by dengue, with numbers much higher than what's seen in any of the 50 states. But in the continental U.S., Florida usually gets the most locally transmitted cases. The state's previous worst year was 2023, when just under 200 locally spread cases were reported. Officials in Hillsborough and surrounding counties have declared local emergencies, and workers in the Tampa area are spraying day and night to tamp down the population of disease-transmitting mosquitoes. Dengue (pronounced DEHN'-gay) is caused by a virus spread by a type of mosquito. Many infected people don't get sick, but some experience fever, flu-like symptoms and — notoriously — aches. It's been nicknamed "breakbone fever" for the excruciating pain some people experience. Severe cases can cause bleeding, shock and death. There has been one dengue death in Florida this year — an elderly Tampa woman on Sept. 4. There are four types of dengue virus, simply known as 1, 2, 3 and 4. When someone is first infected, their body builds antibodies against that type for life. If they get infected with another type of dengue, the antibodies from the first infection may fail to neutralize the second type — and actually can help the virus enter immune cells and replicate. That's made it difficult to develop an effective vaccine. Most people in the Tampa area don't have prior immunity to any form of dengue, said Dawn Wesson, a Tulane University expert on dengue and other diseases spread by mosquitoes. The warm-weather mosquitoes that spread dengue live in Florida and some other hotter U.S. locales, but experts say they have been expanding their geographic reach because of climate change. For decades, most continental U.S. infections were found among people who caught the virus while traveling internationally, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West, Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. The largest outbreak of dengue in any U.S. state since then occurred in Hawaii, where 264 locally acquired cases were reported over a six-month span in 2015-2016. The Tampa-area outbreak, which first came to light in July, is already on the verge of surpassing that. Across the world, more than 2.2 million infections and nearly 1,200 deaths have been reported this year, according to the World Health Organization. There have been nearly 1,900 locally acquired U.S. cases this year, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Florida tends to get a lot of dengue in part because the state receives a lot of travelers who have been to Puerto Rico or other places where the disease is present, Wesson said. Usually most cases are in southern Florida, around the Miami area. It's hard to say what's happening in the Tampa area this year, but the surge may be at least partly related to travel patterns, she added. Locally acquired cases in Florida have actually surpassed travel-associated cases, by a count of 252 to 245 as of last week. But it's close, and at least 13 Hillsborough County cases were diagnosed in travelers, according to the state. Traditionally, the CDC would be highly visible in a situation like this, but it hasn't been this time, Wesson noted. The U.S. public health agency has to be invited in by state officials, however, and Florida officials have not asked for CDC disease investigators to come in, CDC spokesman Jason McDonald said. The agency has provided $800,000 in assistance to the state health department, he added. The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed. People in an outbreak area can take their own steps for protection, experts say. The virus-carrying mosquitoes can bite any time of day, so it's important for people in an outbreak area to apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients like DEET, experts say. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants to cover the skin and make it harder for mosquitoes to bite. Staying indoors, behind screens or in rooms with air conditioning will also lessen the chances for a bite. Those steps are especially important just after sunrise and around sunset, when mosquitoes tend to be most active, researchers say. People should also check their property and get rid of any pooled water where mosquitoes might breed. Climate conditions and persistent mosquito populations will likely make local dengue outbreaks a more frequent problem, Wesson said. "There's a good chance that this is the new normal," she said. ___ The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. State health officials reported this week that more than 250 locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne disease have been tallied so far this year. The vast majority of them were in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Federal health officials say their data on dengue outbreaks is limited. But available information from state health departments and medical journals suggests the Florida outbreak marks the most cases in a calendar year for any state since at least the 1940s. Puerto Rico is consistently hit hard by dengue, with numbers much higher than what's seen in any of the 50 states. But in the continental U.S., Florida usually gets the most locally transmitted cases. The state's previous worst year was 2023, when just under 200 locally spread cases were reported. Officials in Hillsborough and surrounding counties have declared local emergencies, and workers in the Tampa area are spraying day and night to tamp down the population of disease-transmitting mosquitoes. Dengue (pronounced DEHN'-gay) is caused by a virus spread by a type of mosquito. Many infected people don't get sick, but some experience fever, flu-like symptoms and — notoriously — aches. It's been nicknamed "breakbone fever" for the excruciating pain some people experience. Severe cases can cause bleeding, shock and death. There has been one dengue death in Florida this year — an elderly Tampa woman on Sept. 4. There are four types of dengue virus, simply known as 1, 2, 3 and 4. When someone is first infected, their body builds antibodies against that type for life. If they get infected with another type of dengue, the antibodies from the first infection may fail to neutralize the second type — and actually can help the virus enter immune cells and replicate. That's made it difficult to develop an effective vaccine. Most people in the Tampa area don't have prior immunity to any form of dengue, said Dawn Wesson, a Tulane University expert on dengue and other diseases spread by mosquitoes. The warm-weather mosquitoes that spread dengue live in Florida and some other hotter U.S. locales, but experts say they have been expanding their geographic reach because of climate change. For decades, most continental U.S. infections were found among people who caught the virus while traveling internationally, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West, Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. The largest outbreak of dengue in any U.S. state since then occurred in Hawaii, where 264 locally acquired cases were reported over a six-month span in 2015-2016. The Tampa-area outbreak, which first came to light in July, is already on the verge of surpassing that. Across the world, more than 2.2 million infections and nearly 1,200 deaths have been reported this year, according to the World Health Organization. There have been nearly 1,900 locally acquired U.S. cases this year, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Florida tends to get a lot of dengue in part because the state receives a lot of travelers who have been to Puerto Rico or other places where the disease is present, Wesson said. Usually most cases are in southern Florida, around the Miami area. It's hard to say what's happening in the Tampa area this year, but the surge may be at least partly related to travel patterns, she added. Locally acquired cases in Florida have actually surpassed travel-associated cases, by a count of 252 to 245 as of last week. But it's close, and at least 13 Hillsborough County cases were diagnosed in travelers, according to the state. Traditionally, the CDC would be highly visible in a situation like this, but it hasn't been this time, Wesson noted. The U.S. public health agency has to be invited in by state officials, however, and Florida officials have not asked for CDC disease investigators to come in, CDC spokesman Jason McDonald said. The agency has provided $800,000 in assistance to the state health department, he added. The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed. People in an outbreak area can take their own steps for protection, experts say. The virus-carrying mosquitoes can bite any time of day, so it's important for people in an outbreak area to apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients like DEET, experts say. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants to cover the skin and make it harder for mosquitoes to bite. Staying indoors, behind screens or in rooms with air conditioning will also lessen the chances for a bite. Those steps are especially important just after sunrise and around sunset, when mosquitoes tend to be most active, researchers say. People should also check their property and get rid of any pooled water where mosquitoes might breed. Climate conditions and persistent mosquito populations will likely make local dengue outbreaks a more frequent problem, Wesson said. "There's a good chance that this is the new normal," she said. ___ The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations.
