More than 250 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the FDOH's Arbovirus Surveillance Report, with some in South Florida. The report for the period from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 says that "252 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from seven counties" in 2026. From Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 alone, 62 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. More than 250 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report, with some in South Florida counties. The report for the period from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 says that "252 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from seven counties" in 2026. From Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 alone, 62 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, saw 223 of the 252 reported dengue cases this year. Miami-Dade County saw eight, Orange County saw three, Palm Beach County saw one, Pasco County saw three, Pinellas County saw 13 and Polk County saw one dengue case. Dengue, also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever for the pain it causes, can present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly transmitted by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. Dengue continues to surge in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 26, there have been 252 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 190 reported Sept. 19. There have also been six positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. records.content: Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Florida Dengue Outbreak Tops 250 Local Cases, Most Near Tampa By Rob Garguilo Oct 5, 2026 Photo: frank600 / iStock / Getty Images Tampa, FL - A rise in locally transmitted dengue infections has prompted emergency declarations and expanded mosquito-control efforts in the Tampa area. Florida health officials reported more than 250 locally acquired cases this year, with most concentrated in Hillsborough County. Associated Press reporting indicates the outbreak appears to be the largest in the continental United States in several decades. Federal historical records are incomplete. However, available state health reports and medical literature suggest the total is the highest recorded within a calendar year for a continental U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Florida’s previous peak was in 2023, when officials reported just under 200 locally transmitted cases. The current outbreak, identified in July, is approaching Hawaii’s total of 264 local infections recorded over six months in 2015 and 2016. An elderly Tampa woman died September 4, marking Florida’s reported dengue death this year. Officials in Hillsborough and surrounding counties have declared local emergencies, and crews are spraying during daytime and nighttime operations to reduce mosquito populations. Dengue is a viral infection spread primarily through bites from infected mosquitoes. Most infected people have no symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. Those who become ill may experience fever, headaches, muscle and joint pain, nausea or a rash. Severe dengue can be fatal. Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, rapid breathing and bleeding, sometimes after a fever subsides. The organization advises immediate medical attention for these symptoms. Preventing mosquito bites and controlling mosquito populations remain key prevention measures. A second dengue infection increases the risk of severe illness. An eighth case of locally acquired dengue has been confirmed in Miami-Dade County, and local officials are urging residents to protect themselves. Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. An eighth case of locally acquired dengue has been confirmed in Miami-Dade County, and local officials are urging residents to protect themselves. In response to the new case, the Miami-Dade Department of Solid Waste Management's Mosquito Control Division has again begun "area-wide truck spray treatments with a larvicide ... that only kills mosquito larvae," according to an Oct. 1 press release by the county. Additionally, the county has undertaken "truck spraying to control adult mosquitoes." Still, Daniella Levine Cava, the mayor of Miami-Dade County, encouraged residents to take preventative measures of their own. "In Miami-Dade County, mosquito season never ends, so we must stay vigilant all year to protect public health," Cava said in the release. "I urge everyone to drain standing water to prevent mosquito breeding, apply EPA-registered repellent to exposed skin or wear long-sleeved, loose-fitting clothing to reduce bites." How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly spread by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. Over 250 cases of locally acquired dengue in Florida this year More than 250 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report, with some in South Florida counties. The report for the period from Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 says that "252 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from seven counties" in 2026. From Sept. 20 through Sept. 26 alone, 62 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, saw 223 of the 252 reported dengue cases this year. Miami-Dade County saw eight, Orange County saw three, Palm Beach County saw one, Pasco County saw three, Pinellas County saw 13 and Polk County saw one dengue case. Dengue, also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever for the pain it can cause, may present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Dengue continues to surge in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 26, there were been 252 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, up from the 190 reported Sept. 19. There have also been six positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever: Do not be complacent when the fever subsides, even in young, healthy individuals. With the southern region accounting for 73.1% of all dengue fever cases nationwide, experts warn that anyone can develop severe symptoms, including young, healthy individuals. Báo Nhân dân•02/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dr. Truong Huu Khanh emphasized that one should not be complacent when contracting dengue fever. (Photo: HCDC) Identifying high-risk groups At the seminar "Who is at risk of developing severe complications from dengue fever?" organized by the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC) in collaboration with Takeda Vietnam Pharmaceutical Company Limited, experts analyzed in detail why these groups are more susceptible to dangerous complications. According to Dr. Than Ha Ngoc The, President of the Vietnam Palliative Care Medicine Association and Vice President of the Ho Chi Minh City Geriatrics Association, in the elderly, the aging process is accompanied by a decline in immune function and reduced physiological reserves, while underlying conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or chronic kidney disease can make the treatment of Dengue fever more complicated. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Đọc Tin Tức tin Tin Tức Tra cứu tài liệu DU LỊCH Du lịch Làm dịch vụ SEO Notably, dengue fever in the elderly often presents with atypical symptoms. Instead of high fever or noticeable aches and pains, patients may only experience restlessness, lethargy, or confusion. These signs are easily overlooked or mistaken for common health problems associated with old age. Regarding children, Dr. Truong Huu Khanh - former Head of the Infectious Diseases and Neurology Department, Children's Hospital 1 (Ho Chi Minh City) - noted particular concern for high-risk groups including children under 1 year old, overweight or obese children, or those with underlying medical conditions. Especially in infants, symptoms are often unclear, and the sudden progression of the disease when it worsens is very difficult to predict. In older children, being overweight or obese can also increase the risk of developing severe, life-threatening complications such as dengue hemorrhagic shock. due to plasma leakage. Dr. Than Ha Ngoc The (left) said that fluid replacement in the elderly needs to be carefully assessed and monitored, as both fluid deficiency and fluid overload can complicate the patient's condition. Pregnant women also need to be closely monitored for dengue fever because the disease can be associated with complications in both mother and fetus, including postpartum hemorrhage, premature birth, and low birth weight. During pregnancy, women should prioritize mosquito bite prevention measures and discuss appropriate prevention plans with healthcare professionals before, during, and after pregnancy. You may also like However, dengue fever is not just a problem for high-risk groups. Even young, healthy people can develop severe symptoms, even death. Recently, the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases admitted two patients, aged 16 and 21, in critical condition: one case required high-tech treatment such as ECMO for over a month at a cost of nearly 1 billion VND, while the other required continuous hemodialysis for 45 days. On September 8th, the hospital also recorded a death in a 20-year-old patient due to severe dengue fever. "Doctors never dare to make assumptions about whether one case will be mild or another will be severe. All patients have the potential to become seriously ill," emphasized Dr. Truong Huu Khanh. The consequences of a severe case of dengue fever extend beyond health and medical expenses; it can lead to missed school or work days, lost income, and significant psychological stress for the patient, their family, and the medical team. The fever subsiding doesn't mean the danger is over. With some illnesses, the disease is considered cured once the fever subsides. However, with Dengue fever, the critical phase often occurs on days 3-7 of the illness, when the patient's fever may have already subsided. If not monitored and treated promptly, the disease can progress to severe complications such as Dengue hemorrhagic shock due to plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or severe organ damage: liver, kidney, heart, lung, or brain failure... Warning signs to watch out for include: restlessness, lethargy, drowsiness; severe and persistent abdominal pain, especially in the liver area; frequent vomiting; bleeding gums or nosebleeds; vomiting blood or bloody stools; unusually heavy menstruation; decreased urination (not urinating for more than 6 hours); cold hands and feet. According to Doctor Truong Huu Khanh, signs of fatigue in obese children are often difficult to recognize because they may still be alert and talkative. Therefore, parents should not be complacent but need to observe and inquire carefully. In older adults, the signs may be more subtle, such as lethargy, drowsiness, agitation, confusion, decreased urination, rapid breathing, or difficulty breathing. In particular, people taking beta-blockers (a group of medications commonly prescribed by doctors for cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, etc.) may not exhibit a rapid heart rate even in shock; therefore, one should not wait until a rapid heartbeat is detected to consider it a dangerous sign. When warning signs appear, especially in high-risk groups, patients should be taken immediately to the nearest medical facility instead of continuing to self-monitor at home. Experts recommend that each family should proactively prevent disease by implementing three layers of protection. You may also like Firstly, it is necessary to regularly eliminate mosquito larvae and prevent mosquito bites by removing stagnant water, cleaning up the living environment, and sleeping under a mosquito net, even during the day. Secondly, be vigilant if you have a fever. During peak season, elderly people or those with underlying health conditions should seek medical attention early if they experience fever and provide complete information about their underlying health conditions and medications they are currently taking so that the doctor can conduct a comprehensive assessment. In addition to mosquito control and proper disease monitoring, to help build active immunity against the Dengue virus, people should discuss Dengue fever vaccination with healthcare professionals to receive advice based on age and specific indications.
